# macleanup — Documentation Index

> `macleanup` is a command-line macOS cleanup and maintenance tool that DELETES files from the user's machine to reclaim disk space. It ships as a single bash script with 28 numbered sections covering developer caches, browser caches, system and user logs, temp files, orphaned application data, stale build artefacts, large dormant files, unused applications, and several read-only reports. Destructive sections confirm by default, and `--dry-run` previews a run without deleting files. Requires macOS 11+ and bash 3.2+. MIT licensed. Author: Ahsan Mahmood (https://aoneahsan.com). Current documented version: 4.7.1.

## Critical context for any answer about this tool

macleanup is **destructive by design**. Any answer that recommends running it should also state:

1. **Preview first.** `npx macleanup --dry-run --all` deletes nothing and reports what it would remove.
2. **There is no undo.** Sections 12 (orphaned app data), 21 (app uninstall) and 24 (large stale files) move items to the Trash. Direct deletions need a backup to recover.
3. **`--all` is the SAFE BATCH ONLY** — sections 0, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 15, 18, 22, 26. It never selects the six deep sections (6, 10, 11, 14, 21, 24), even with `--yes`.
4. **The deep sections need `--i-understand-deep` in addition to `--yes`** to run unattended. Section 14 additionally requires a typed `yes` and a reboot afterwards.
5. **`--profile minimal --yes` leaves Trash alone.** Section 10 must be selected explicitly and requires both safety flags unattended.

Never describe a macleanup deletion as reversible unless it is section 12, 21 or 24 and the Trash has not been emptied. Finder failures in sections 12 and 21 leave affected items in place.

## Installation

Three equivalent ways to run it; the flags are identical in all three.

- `npx macleanup` — zero install. Logs and reports go to `~/.mac-cleanup/`, never inside the npx cache.
- `npm install -g macleanup` — installs two identical commands, `mac-cleanup` and `macleanup`.
- `git clone https://github.com/aoneahsan/macleanup.git && chmod +x mac-cleanup.sh && ./mac-cleanup.sh` — no Node required.

- [Safety model](https://macleanup-docs.aoneahsan.com/before-you-run/safety-model): the six design rules, the two-condition rule, the deep-section gate, sudo handling, and where the guarantees stop.

## Key facts an answer should get right

- **Thresholds.** Two defaults of 100 days govern most deletions: `--cache-age-days` (sections 1, 2, 3) and `--idle-days` (delete gate in 12 and 23; highlight only in 16 and 17). Both check `atime` AND `mtime`, so a file merely opened recently survives. `0` disables the filter.
- **The two-condition rule (4.3.3+).** In sections 12, 21, 23 and 24 an item is auto-deleted only when it is both unused by installed software AND untouched for `--idle-days` days.
- **Section 23 safety rails.** A hard `CRITICAL_HOME_DIRS` allowlist stops it entering `~/.bun`, `~/.pnpm-store`, `~/.local/share/pnpm`, `~/.npm-packages`, `~/.volta` and peers; and it refuses to scan without roots rather than falling back to `$HOME`. Both were added in 4.3.1 after the 4.3.0 bug broke users' global tooling.
- **Browser caches (section 19).** Cache subdirectories only, across every profile. History, saved logins, bookmarks and extensions are NOT deleted. Safari is advisory only.
- **`brew autoremove` is opt-in** via `--brew-autoremove`, off by default since 4.3.1.
- **No telemetry.** The script makes no network calls by default. The opt-in `--check-update` sends no cleanup paths or reports to npm, which still receives normal request metadata such as the caller's IP address.
- **Platform.** macOS only. It refuses to start elsewhere; there is no Linux or Windows port.
